meta.blurb: Noor is a baker who is always hungry by four o'clock, and her neighbour Ines is a retired nurse. Together they follow the body's hunger signals, from the stomach to the brain, and learn what science knows and what it does not.
meta.bible: Noor: a baker in her thirties who runs a small bakery and is often hungry in the afternoon. Ines: her neighbour, a retired nurse, calm and clear, who explains general science. They talk in the bakery kitchen and in Ines's Garden over about Three weeks. Key terms: Hormones, Hormone, Hypothalamus, Ghrelin, Leptin, Insulin, Pancreas, Glucose, Cortisol, Dopamine, Thyroid, Peptide, Cholecystokinin, Fibre, Protein, Appetite, Metabolism, Diabetes, Stigma. Real science only, hedged where research is unsettled: no invented numbers or studies. Voice: warm, calm, plain, curious, never blaming. Nobody gets personal medical advice; the book gives general information and tells readers to see a doctor about their own health. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: Noor is a baker, and she is hungry again, even though she ate a big dinner. She wonders why her body keeps asking for food when she has so much to do.
Ines used to be a nurse, and she drops in for bread most mornings. She tells Noor that hunger is not a weakness but a message from the body.
The body uses two main ways to send messages: nerves and hormones. Hormones are chemicals that travel through the blood to tell different parts of the body what to do.
Deep in the brain sits a small area called the hypothalamus. It is a little like a control room, because it listens to signals about food and energy from all over the body.
Scientists often separate hunger from appetite, and the two are not the same. Hunger is the body's need for fuel, while appetite is the wish to eat, which a smell or a habit can set off.
The first hormone to meet is ghrelin, which is made mostly in the stomach. When the stomach has been empty for a while, more ghrelin goes into the blood and travels to the brain.
Studies suggest that ghrelin does not only rise when we have gone without food. It also tends to rise around the times we normally eat, because the body learns our daily routine.
After a meal, the level of ghrelin falls again, and the hungry feeling slowly fades. How far it falls can depend on what was eaten and how much of it.
Hunger is not only about the stomach, because fat tissue matters too. It makes a hormone called leptin, which tells the brain roughly how much energy the body has stored.
If the body loses a lot of fat, leptin levels fall, and the brain responds by turning up hunger. This is the body's way of protecting itself from running out of fuel.
Ines reminds Noor that body fat is not an enemy. It stores energy, keeps the body warm, protects the organs and helps to make some hormones.
Next comes insulin, which is made by the pancreas, a long, flat organ tucked behind the stomach. The pancreas releases insulin into the blood when we eat.
When we eat food that contains carbohydrate, the body breaks it into glucose, a kind of sugar. The level of glucose in the blood rises, and a short while later it comes down again.
Insulin acts a little like a key that opens the door of a cell. It helps the muscles, the liver and the fat tissue to take glucose out of the blood and use it.
Insulin does more than lower blood sugar, because it also helps to store energy for later. Energy that is not needed right away is kept in the liver and muscles or as fat.
In people with diabetes, the body either makes too little insulin or cannot respond to it well. Doctors can test for this and treat it, so Ines tells Noor to see a doctor if she is worried.
Not all foods act in the same way when they reach the gut. Foods with a lot of fibre, such as beans, are digested slowly, so blood sugar rises more gently than after a sugary drink.

Protein, which is found in eggs, fish, beans and meat, has a reputation for filling people up. Many studies agree that it tends to keep people satisfied for longer than the same amount of other foods.
The gut also sends messages after a meal, as food moves through the intestine. Hormones such as peptide YY and cholecystokinin tell the brain that it is time to stop.
Hormones are only half of the story, because nerves help as well. When the stomach stretches with food, a long nerve called the vagus carries the news to the brain.

Fullness signals do not arrive at once, and it can take some time for them to build up. Eating more slowly may give the body a better chance to notice that it has had enough, although the evidence is modest.
Another gut hormone is called GLP-1, and it is released after eating. It helps the pancreas to make the right amount of insulin, slows the stomach and tells the brain that the body is satisfied.

Scientists have made medicines that copy GLP-1, and some people take them for diabetes or for weight loss. They are prescribed by doctors, they can have side effects, and they are not suitable for everyone.
Noor was so busy with customers that she had no lunch. By four o'clock she feels shaky and cross, and she eats three biscuits before she even thinks about it.
Noor admits that she sleeps badly when she gets up at four. Small studies suggest that short sleep can raise ghrelin, lower leptin and increase appetite, although the size of the effect varies.
When Noor is under stress, her body releases cortisol. This hormone gets the body ready to cope, and in some people it can increase the wish to eat, especially tasty foods.
Cortisol is not only a stress hormone, because it also follows a daily rhythm. Its level is highest soon after waking and lowest around midnight, and it helps us to wake up.
People sometimes eat because they feel sad, bored or lonely, and not because their body needs fuel. Tasty food activates the brain's reward system, which uses a chemical called dopamine.
Researchers think that dopamine is more about wanting than about enjoying. That is why the smell of baking or a picture of a doughnut can pull on us even when we are not hungry.
For most of history, food was hard to find, and the body is built to cope with shortages. Today tasty, cheap food is everywhere, and that can make it easy for people to eat more than they need.

In one careful study, volunteers lived in a research centre and ate either ultra-processed or unprocessed meals. On the processed diet they ate faster and took in more calories, but it was a small study and not the last word.
At the front of the neck sits the thyroid gland, which makes hormones that help to set how fast the body uses energy. If it works too slowly or too quickly, a doctor can test for it.
Hormones change during a person's life, in puberty, in pregnancy and at the menopause. These changes can alter appetite and where the body stores fat, and they are normal parts of life.

Genes shape how strongly our hunger signals work and how easily the body stores fat. Studies of families and twins suggest that body weight is partly inherited, so two people can eat alike and still look different.
Noor asks whether it is all down to willpower, and Ines says no. Biology has a strong say, but habits, surroundings and daily choices still count, and a person can often change those.

Researchers have found that after a person loses weight, leptin tends to fall and ghrelin tends to rise. The body behaves as if it wants the weight back, which helps to explain why regaining it is so common.
Some scientists believe that the body defends a range of weight, a little like a thermostat. Others think that the idea is too simple, and the debate is not settled.

Some people try eating only during a short window of the day. The research on this is mixed, and it is not suitable for everyone, including children, pregnant women and people who take diabetes medicine.
Ines also mentions that some people have an eating disorder, which is a serious illness and not a choice. If food and weight take over someone's thoughts, doctors and special services can help.

Some medicines change appetite, including certain steroids and drugs for mood or sleep. Ines says that no one should stop a medicine alone, and that anyone who is worried should speak to a doctor or pharmacist.

Ines explains that very strong, constant hunger can sometimes be a sign of illness, especially if it comes with great thirst, tiredness or weight loss. In that case, she says, the right step is to see a doctor.
Noor decides to keep a small notebook by the till. Each time she eats, she writes down how hungry she was, what she ate and how she felt an hour later.
Noor tries eating a proper breakfast, with eggs, oats and fruit. For her, the afternoons feel calmer, although Ines warns that what works for one person does not always work for another.
Noor starts to walk after work, and it clears her head. Exercise has complicated effects on appetite, but it helps muscles to use glucose, and many people find that it improves sleep and mood.

Ines admits that scientists still argue about some big questions, such as why people gain weight. Some stress the calories we eat, others stress hormones such as insulin, and many believe that both matter.

Ines says that weight stigma, which means judging people harshly for their size, is not only unkind but harmful. Health depends on many things, and a number on a scale tells only a small part of the story.
Ines adds a note about children, whose bodies are growing fast. They need plenty of food, and a child should only follow a special diet if a doctor has advised it.

Ines helps Noor to see the whole picture, and she describes the hormones as a team. Ghrelin pushes her to eat, leptin reports on her stores, insulin manages fuel, and the gut hormones help her to stop.
Noor finds that she is no longer angry with her body. When her customers ask why she looks so thoughtful, she tells them what she has learned, and some of them tell her their own stories.

This book has given general information about hormones and hunger, and the science is still growing. It is not medical advice, so anyone with worries about their own health or weight should talk to a doctor.
C1C2: Before the sun had properly risen, Noor was already in the bakery kitchen, shaping dough with floury hands and listening to her stomach complain. She had eaten a generous dinner only a few hours earlier, and yet here was that familiar, hollow feeling again. It occurred to her, for the first time, that hunger was a mystery she had lived with all her life without ever asking what it was.

Ines, who had spent thirty years as a nurse before retiring to the flat next door, called in for her usual loaf and found Noor frowning at the oven. She listened to the worry, smiled, and said that hunger is not a character flaw but a message, one that the body has been sending since the day we were born. Then she added that a message is easier to understand once you know who is sending it and why.

The body keeps in touch with itself in two main ways: through nerves, which carry quick electrical signals, and through hormones, which are chemical messengers released into the blood. Glands and organs make these substances in tiny amounts, and they travel around the body until they reach the cells that know how to read them. Appetite, growth, sleep, mood and the way we use energy are all steered by this quiet and constant conversation.

Deep inside the brain, about the size of an almond, lies a region called the hypothalamus, and it acts rather like a control room for hunger. Signals about food, fat stores, blood sugar and stress flow into it from every direction, and it weighs them together before the rest of the brain is told how hungry we feel. No single signal makes the decision alone, which is one reason why appetite is so hard to switch off by willpower.

Researchers like to distinguish hunger, which is the body's genuine call for fuel, from appetite, which is the desire to eat and may have little to do with fuel at all. A trail of warm bread drifting across the kitchen, a favourite song on the radio, or the simple fact that it is half past three can awaken an appetite in someone who has only just eaten. Noticing which of the two is speaking turns out to be the first useful skill in understanding our own eating.

The first hormone worth knowing is ghrelin, which is produced mainly by cells in the lining of the stomach. When the stomach has been empty for some hours, the level of ghrelin in the blood climbs, and the hypothalamus reads that rise as a request for food. Because of this, ghrelin is often called the hunger hormone, although the name rather simplifies a subtle and many-sided story.

One of the more curious findings is that ghrelin does not simply track an empty stomach, since in many people it begins to climb shortly before the times of day at which they habitually eat. The body, it seems, learns the rhythm of our meals and prepares in advance, much as a dog learns the sound of its owner's key in the door. This helps to explain why Noor feels most hungry at the very hour that lunch has always happened, whether or not she is short of fuel.

Once food reaches the stomach and gut, the level of ghrelin falls back, and the urgent pull of hunger gradually loosens its grip. How much it drops, and for how long, appears to depend on what was eaten and in what quantity, which is why two meals with the same calories can leave a person feeling quite different. Scientists are still mapping these differences, and they caution that results from one small study do not always hold for everyone.

Hunger is not decided by the stomach alone, because body fat is itself a kind of gland, and it releases a hormone known as leptin. The more fat tissue a person has, the more leptin tends to circulate, and the hypothalamus reads it as a report on how much energy is kept in store. It is a slow, long-term signal, closer to a fuel gauge on a dashboard than to the sudden rumble of an empty belly.

When the body's fat stores shrink, the amount of leptin in the blood drops as well, and the brain interprets the fall as a warning that energy is running short. Its response is to increase hunger, to make food seem more attractive and, in some cases, to slow the rate at which energy is spent. From the point of view of our ancestors, who lived with real shortages, this was a sensible protection rather than a design fault.

Ines is quick to point out that body fat has been given a bad reputation it does not entirely deserve. It stores energy for lean days, cushions and protects the organs, helps to keep the body warm and takes part in making several hormones, so a certain amount of it is essential for health. The real questions, she says, concern how much is healthy for a particular person, and doctors are the right people to ask.

The next hormone on Ines's list is insulin, which is made by the pancreas, a long and flat organ tucked in behind the stomach. Special cells inside it measure the sugar in the blood, and when a meal pushes that sugar upwards they release insulin in proportion to what they sense. It is one of the most important hormones we have, and it has been studied closely for over a century.

Foods that contain carbohydrate, such as bread, rice, fruit and potatoes, are broken down in the gut into glucose, the simple sugar that cells use as fuel. The level of glucose in the blood then rises for a while, reaches a peak, and gradually returns to where it began, tracing a shape like a gentle hill. How steep that hill is depends on the food, on the person and on what else was eaten at the same meal.

Insulin works rather like a key, signalling to the cells of the muscles, the liver and the fat tissue that they should open up and take glucose in from the blood. Once the sugar has been absorbed, the cells burn it for immediate energy or put it aside, and the level in the bloodstream falls back toward normal. In a healthy body this adjustment happens all day long without anyone noticing it.

Besides lowering blood sugar, insulin encourages the body to store energy that is not needed at once, packing some into the liver and muscles as a starch called glycogen and the rest into fat. This is entirely normal, and it is what allows us to go for hours between meals without our brains running out of fuel. Problems arise only when the system stops working as it should, and that is a matter for doctors rather than for guessing.

In diabetes, the system that keeps blood sugar steady has broken down: in type one the pancreas makes almost no insulin, while in type two the body makes it but its cells respond poorly. Both conditions are serious but manageable, and they are diagnosed with simple blood tests and treated under the guidance of a doctor. Ines is careful to say that she is describing the basic idea, and that anyone worried about their own health should speak to a medical professional.

Different foods push blood sugar up at very different speeds, and the amount of fibre is one of the main reasons. A sugary drink is absorbed almost at once, whereas a plate of lentils and vegetables must be broken down slowly, so the glucose reaches the blood in a gentle trickle instead of a rush. Nutrition scientists disagree about how much this matters for health in the long run, but the basic difference in speed is well established.

Protein, which is found in eggs, fish, dairy products, beans and meat, has a good reputation for satisfying hunger, and many studies back it up. It appears to affect several of the gut hormones at once and to take the body more effort to digest, so a meal rich in it often keeps people feeling full for longer. The effect varies from person to person, however, and nobody should treat it as a magic rule.

After a meal, the intestines release a whole group of hormones, among them peptide YY and cholecystokinin, which report on what has just arrived. They slow the movement of food through the gut and send a message to the brain that energy is on its way, so the desire to keep eating gradually fades. Scientists often think of them as the brake pedal, to set beside the accelerator that ghrelin seems to provide.

Hormones are only half the story, for the stomach wall is also full of tiny sensors that respond when it stretches. They pass the news up a long nerve called the vagus, which runs from the gut to the brain, and the brain combines it with the chemical signals arriving through the blood. The whole system is built so that no single message is trusted entirely, much like a pilot who checks several instruments before landing.

The signals of fullness do not arrive the moment food is swallowed, and they can take a good while to build up in the blood and the nerves. A person who eats very fast may therefore finish a large portion before the brain has been told how much has actually arrived. Some studies suggest that eating more slowly helps people to feel full on less, though the evidence is modest and the effect is probably small.

A further gut hormone, usually shortened to GLP-1, is released by cells in the intestine as soon as food arrives. It prompts the pancreas to release insulin when it is needed, slows the rate at which the stomach empties, and sends a message of satisfaction to the brain. Its discovery has been one of the most important developments in the modern understanding of appetite.

Researchers have designed medicines that imitate GLP-1, and in recent years doctors have prescribed them to people with type two diabetes and to some people living with obesity. They can reduce appetite considerably, but they also carry side effects and risks, they are not suitable for everyone, and they must be chosen and monitored by a doctor. Noor is curious about them, but Ines gently reminds her that such decisions belong in a medical appointment, not in a bakery kitchen.

The shop had been unusually busy, and Noor had worked right through the lunch hour without a single bite. By four o'clock her head was light, her temper short and her hands slightly shaky, and before she had thought about it she had eaten three biscuits standing up. Ines, who happened to be passing, told her that this was exactly the kind of moment in which the body's signals deserve a little respect.

Noor confesses that she is awake long before sunrise most days, and that she is hungrier in the afternoon when she has slept badly. Ines tells her that several small experiments have found that people who sleep for only a few hours tend to have more ghrelin, less leptin and a stronger appetite for sweet, starchy food. The results are not identical in every study, and they involve only a few people each time, but they fit what many tired people report.

During stressful moments, such as a long queue and a broken oven, the adrenal glands release a hormone called cortisol, which prepares the body to cope with a threat. Over a short time it can actually reduce appetite, but when stress lasts for weeks it seems to push many people toward eating more, and especially toward rich and sugary foods. Researchers stress that people differ a great deal, and that some eat less than usual when they are under pressure.

Cortisol is not simply an emergency chemical, because its level follows a daily rhythm that is highest soon after we wake and lowest in the middle of the night. This morning peak helps to raise blood sugar and alertness, so that the body is ready for the day, and the evening decline helps it to prepare for sleep. When stress, shift work or poor sleep disturb the rhythm, appetite and mood may be affected too.

Many of us eat at times when the body does not need fuel at all, because we are sad, bored, lonely or simply tired. Tasty food activates the brain's reward system, which uses a chemical messenger called dopamine, and the pleasant feeling that follows can teach the brain to reach for the same food again. This is a normal part of being human, and there is nothing shameful about it.

Researchers who study the brain believe that dopamine has more to do with wanting something than with enjoying it once it has arrived. This explains why a poster of a glistening doughnut or the smell of baking from an open door can pull on us strongly even when we have just eaten. Businesses know this very well, and a large part of food advertising is designed to make that pull as strong as possible.

For most of human history, food was scarce and getting enough of it took real effort, and our bodies evolved to cope with shortage far better than with plenty. Today, cheap, rich and heavily marketed food is available at nearly every corner, and our ancient hormonal systems were never designed for that situation. Seen in this light, finding it hard to resist is not a personal failure but a mismatch between old biology and a new environment.

In one carefully controlled experiment, a small group of volunteers lived in a research centre for several weeks, eating a diet of ultra-processed food for two weeks and a diet of unprocessed food for two weeks. When the meals were ultra-processed, they ate more quickly and took in several hundred extra calories a day, even though they were free to eat as much as they liked. It was a small study, however, so scientists treat it as an interesting clue rather than a final answer.

At the front of the neck sits the thyroid, a small butterfly-shaped gland whose hormones help to set the speed at which the body uses energy. If the gland is underactive, a person may feel tired, cold and heavy, and if it is overactive they may feel restless, hot and unusually hungry. These conditions are common enough, and they can be found with a simple blood test and treated by a doctor.

Hormone levels change a great deal across a lifetime, notably during puberty, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and at the menopause, when the ovaries produce much less oestrogen. These changes can alter appetite, energy and the places where the body stores fat, and they are perfectly normal stages in the life of a human being. If the changes are hard to live with, doctors can offer help and advice.

Genes influence how strongly the hunger signals work, how readily the body stores fat and how rewarding certain foods feel, and studies of families and twins show that body weight is substantially inherited. Two people may therefore eat in a similar way and still differ in size, without either of them being lazier or more disciplined than the other. It is a humbling piece of knowledge, and it ought to make us slow to judge anyone's body.

Noor asks, a little sadly, whether it all comes down to willpower in the end. Ines answers that willpower matters much less than most people think, since the body's own signals can be very strong, but that habits, surroundings and daily routines have a real effect and can sometimes be changed. Biology, in other words, is the weather we live in, and habits are the way we dress for it.

Studies of people who have lost a good deal of weight show that their leptin level tends to fall and their ghrelin level tends to rise, and that these changes can last for a year or more. The body, it seems, behaves as though it has been threatened with famine, which helps to explain why so many people who diet find that the weight comes back. This is biology at work, not a lack of character, and it deserves sympathy rather than blame.

Some scientists propose that the brain defends a range of body weight, much as a thermostat holds a room at a steady temperature, and they call it the set point. Others argue that the idea is too simple, because weight clearly shifts with food supply, age and surroundings over the years. The question is still being studied, and an honest answer must admit that the experts do not agree.

Many people have tried eating only within a short window of the day, and the practice has become very popular. The research so far is mixed, with some studies finding benefits and others finding no more than ordinary calorie cutting, and it is not suitable for everyone, including children, pregnant women and people who take medicine for diabetes. Ines advises anyone who is curious to talk to their doctor before they change how they eat.

Ines pauses to say something important: some people live with an eating disorder, which is a serious illness of the mind and body and not a matter of choice or vanity. If thoughts about food, eating or weight begin to take over a person's life, they should speak to a doctor, because effective help exists and recovery is possible. She adds that no one needs to wait until things are very bad before they ask.

Certain medicines can make people hungrier or less hungry as a side effect, among them some steroids and some drugs prescribed for mood, sleep or other conditions. Ines is firm that nobody should stop a prescribed medicine on their own because of this, since the risks of stopping can be greater than the side effect itself. Anyone who is troubled by a change in appetite should talk to a doctor or pharmacist, who can look at the whole picture.

Ines explains that although most hunger is perfectly ordinary, extreme and constant hunger can occasionally be a sign of illness, particularly when it comes with great thirst, unusual tiredness or loss of weight without trying. Conditions such as diabetes and an overactive thyroid can cause these symptoms, and both can be found with simple tests. She tells Noor that if this ever happens, the sensible step is to see a doctor rather than to wait and wonder.

Rather than guess, Noor decides to keep a small notebook behind the till, in which she records how hungry she was before each meal, what she ate and how she felt about an hour afterwards. It is a tiny experiment, and it cannot prove anything about the body in general, but it helps her to notice her own patterns, which are often invisible when she is rushing. Within days she has found that her worst afternoons always follow the mornings on which she skipped breakfast.

Encouraged by her notes, Noor begins to take her time over breakfast, eating eggs, oats and fruit instead of a roll grabbed on the run. She finds the afternoons calmer and the biscuits less tempting, though Ines warns her not to turn one person's experience into a rule for everyone. What steadies one body, she says, may do nothing at all for the next, and only patient trial can tell us which is which.

Noor begins to walk briskly for half an hour after closing the shop, and she is surprised by how much it clears her head. Exercise has complicated and sometimes opposite effects on appetite hormones, depending on its type and length, but it helps the muscles to take up glucose and it improves sleep and mood for many people. Ines is happy to add that the benefits do not depend on losing any weight at all.

Ines admits that the experts have not settled some of the biggest questions, such as why bodies gain weight. Some emphasise how many calories we eat and burn, others place hormones like insulin at the centre of the story, and a good number believe that both matter, together with sleep, stress, genes, medicines and surroundings. The honest position, she says, is that a simple single cause is unlikely, and anyone who sells one should be treated with caution.

Ines speaks seriously about weight stigma, the habit of judging and mocking people because of the size of their bodies. Research suggests that shame does not help people to look after themselves and may well make things worse, and that health depends on many things, such as sleep, movement, food, stress, income and genes. A number on the scales is only one of them, and kindness, she says, is not the opposite of science but a part of good practice.

Ines adds a short note about children, whose bodies are in a period of rapid growth and need generous amounts of energy and nutrients. Restricting their food, or talking about their bodies in a worried way, can do more harm than good, and a child should follow a special diet only when a doctor has advised it. She says that the best gift an adult can give is a calm, regular and friendly table.

Over tea, Ines helps Noor to pull the pieces together into a single picture of a team at work. Ghrelin nudges the body toward food, leptin reports on the energy in store, insulin manages the sugar, and the gut hormones help us to stop. Sleep, stress, habit and surroundings keep adjusting the volume of every one of them, and listening to such a conversation takes practice.

By the end of three weeks, Noor realised that she had stopped being angry with her own stomach, and that she now heard its rumbling as a message to be understood and not as a verdict to be feared. When customers asked why she looked so thoughtful, she told them a little of what Ines had taught her, and several of them offered stories of their own across the counter. The bakery, it seemed, had become a place where people could talk about hunger without any shame.

Noor and Ines sat quietly in the garden as the evening light faded, and the story of hunger felt less like a puzzle and more like a conversation worth continuing. This book has offered only general information, and the science it describes is still developing, so it is not medical advice and cannot replace the care of a doctor who knows you. If you are worried about your appetite, your weight or your health, please speak to a medical professional, who can look at your own situation with the attention it deserves.
